facts.fact_text: [F1] $\Phi_+=\{\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{nh/2}\}$ with the $\rho_i$ pairwise distinct and $\rho_{i+n}=C\rho_i$, $\mu_{i+n}=C\mu_i$ for all $i\ge1$, where $C:=\rho(c)$; $C-\mathrm{id}$ is invertible, $\mu(\rho_i)=\mu_i$, and $M(c)=V$. Hence $\ell_T(c)=n$. [[lem-cg-steinberg-bipartite-root-enumeration]] (1)-(4) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.2: 1.2 For all $i,j\ge1$, $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i$. Indeed, $\rho_i=\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)$ by [F2], so $-\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-C\mu_j\cdot\tfrac12(\mu_i-C\mu_i)=\tfrac12(\mu_j-C\mu_j)\cdot\mu_i=\rho_j\cdot\mu_i$, using the isometry of $C$ and [F1]-[F2]. This is (2)(a). [F1, F2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.3: 1.3 Suppose $1\le i\le j\le nh/2$. If $i>n$, then $j>n$ and $C$-equivariance gives $\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=\mu_{i-n}\cdot\rho_{j-n}$. Repeating reduces to a first index at most $n$ while keeping both indices positive and ordered. For $i\le n$, $\mu_i=\beta_i$, and $\beta_i\cdot\rho_j$ is the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ in the positive root $\rho_j$; this is nonnegative by [F4]. Thus (2)(b) holds. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.2.1: 2.1 To prove (2)(c), first reduce $i$ modulo $n$ using $C$-equivariance, which preserves $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i$, and assume $1\le i\le n$. If $i+t\le n$, then $\mu_{i+t}=\beta_{i+t}$ and $\rho_i=R_1\cdots R_{i-1}\alpha_i$ has no $\alpha_{i+t}$ coefficient, so the pairing is zero. If $i+t>n$, put $j=i+t-n$, so $1\le j<i$. By (2)(a), $\mu_{i+t}\cdot\rho_i=\mu_{j+n}\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_i\cdot\rho_j=-\beta_i\cdot\rho_j=0$, since $\rho_j$ is supported on $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_j$. Now if $1\le i<j\le nh/2$ and $j<i+n$, (2)(d) is (2)(c) with $t=j-i$; if $j\ge i+n$, (2)(a) and (2)(b) give $\mu_j\cdot\rho_i=-\mu_{i+n}\cdot\rho_j\le0$. This proves (2)(c)-(d). [F1, F2, F4, step 1.3, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.2: 4.2 In any such positive root subsystem with simple system $\Gamma$, its first root in the global order is a member of $\Gamma$. For if the first root $\eta$ were not simple, write $\eta=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}b_\gamma\gamma$ with $b_\gamma\ge0$; each $\gamma$ is later than $\eta$, so (2)(d) gives $\mu(\gamma)\cdot\eta\le0$. Linearity of $\mu$ and (1) would give $1=\mu(\eta)\cdot\eta=\sum b_\gamma(\mu(\gamma)\cdot\eta)\le0$, impossible. Also the last root of $P_\sigma$ belongs to $\Delta$: otherwise it is a nonnegative combination of the earlier simple roots, contrary to step 3.1. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1:
6.1 Let $q$ be the global index with $\delta_k=ho_q$ and put $
u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $
u\cdotho_j=\mu_{q+n}\cdotho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdotho_{q+n}=-\mu_j\cdotho_q\le0$ by (2)(b); at $j=q$ this is $-1$. Since $\mu_q\in F(r c)$, conjugating by $C$ gives $
u\in F(c r)$; and $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$, so $F(cr)=\mathbb R
u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$ and $
u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $
u\cdot\delta_j=0$. Those zero-pairing simple roots must span the $(k-1)$-space $U$, so they are exactly $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{k-1}$. They form a simple system for $P_{\sigma'}$. Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F5] Carter's formula gives $\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)$; $u\le_Tv$ iff $\ell_T(v)=\ell_T(u)+\ell_T(u^{-1}v)$; $u\le_Tv$ implies $M(u)\subseteq M(v)$; if $u,v\le_Tc$, then $u\le_Tv$ iff $M(u)\subseteq M(v)$; and $\ell_T$ is invariant under conjugation and satisfies the triangle inequality. [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1)-(3)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 We prove the recursive selection and the factorization $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$ by induction on $k$. For $k=1$, $W_\sigma$ has rank one, $P_\sigma$ has its single positive root $\delta_1$, and $\sigma=R(\delta_1)$. For $k>1$, order the simple roots increasingly; step 4.2 makes the last one $\delta_k=\tau_t$. Put $r=R(\delta_k)$. Since $r\le_T\sigma$, write $\sigma=ru$ with $\ell_T(u)=k-1$; then $\sigma':=\sigma r=rur$ has length $k-1$. Write $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$. The identity $c=\sigma'(rv)$ and the bounds $\ell_T(rv)\le n-k+1$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(\sigma')+\ell_T(rv)$ force $\ell_T(rv)=n-k+1$, so $\sigma'\le_Tc$. Also $\sigma'$ fixes $F$ pointwise, hence $M(\sigma')\subseteq E$. [F5, step 1.4, step 1.6, step 4.1, step 4.2]
proof_step_texts.6.1:
6.1 Let $q$ be the global index with $\delta_k=ho_q$ and put $
u=C\mu_q=\mu_{q+n}$. For every $ho_j\in P_\sigma$ one has $j\le q$ and, by (2)(a) and $C$-equivariance, $
u\cdotho_j=\mu_{q+n}\cdotho_j=-\mu_{j+n}\cdotho_{q+n}=-\mu_j\cdotho_q\le0$ by (2)(b); at $j=q$ this is $-1$. Since $\mu_q\in F(r c)$, conjugating by $C$ gives $
u\in F(c r)$; and $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$, so $F(cr)=\mathbb R
u$ and $M(cr)=
u^\perp$. Moreover $\sigma'\le_Tc r$: its complement is $\sigma'^{-1}cr=rvr$, of length $n-k$, while $\ell_T(cr)=n-1$; the lengths add to $n-1$. Hence $U:=M(\sigma')$ is contained in $E\cap
u^\perp$, and both have dimension $k-1$ because $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$. Thus $U=E\cap
u^\perp$. The roots $P_{\sigma'}=\Phi_+\cap U$ span $U$ by step 2.2. Each is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and is orthogonal to $
u$; since $
u\cdot\delta_k=-1$ and $
u\cdot\delta_j\le0$ for every $j$, every root in $P_{\sigma'}$ is a combination only of the $\delta_j$ for which $
u\cdot\delta_j=0$. Those zero-pairing simple roots must span the $(k-1)$-space $U$, so they are exactly $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{k-1}$. They form a simple system for $P_{\sigma'}$. Induction gives $\sigma'=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{k-1})$ and proves the reverse selection at each rank. Therefore $\sigma=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. For each $i$, its prefix $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ and complementary suffix $R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)$ multiply to $\sigma$ and have at most $i$ and $k-i$ reflections, so both lengths attain these bounds. Thus $M(p_i)$, contained in $\operatorname{span}(\delta_1,\dots,\delta_i)$, has dimension $i$ and equals that span. Since $\sigma R(\delta_k)\cdots R(\delta_{i+1})=p_i$, the induction shows that $\delta_i$ is the last root of $P_\sigma$ in this subspace. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 5.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.1: 7.1 The other recursive description follows by considering the suffix $q_i:=R(\delta_i)\cdots R(\delta_k)$. The factorization in step 6.1 gives $\ell_T(q_i)=k-i+1$: its prefix and suffix factors together multiply to $\sigma$ of length $k$, and their lengths are bounded by their numbers of reflections, whose sum is $k$. Writing $p_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$, the same length equality forces $\ell_T(p_i)=i-1$, so $q_i^{-1}\sigma=q_i^{-1}p_iq_i$ has length $i-1$ and $q_i\le_T\sigma$. If $c=\sigma v$ as above, then $q_i^{-1}c=q_i^{-1}(R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1}))q_i v$ has length at most $(i-1)+(n-k)=n-\ell_T(q_i)$; the triangle inequality forces equality, so $q_i\le_Tc$. Its moved space is $\operatorname{span}(\delta_i,\dots,\delta_k)$, since its factors fix the orthogonal complement of that span and its moved dimension is $k-i+1$. Thus $P_{q_i}=P_\sigma\cap M(q_i)$, and $\{\delta_i,\dots,\delta_k\}$ is a simple system for this subsystem: a root in the tail span has zero coefficients on $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$ in its nonnegative $\Delta$-expansion. By step 4.2 the first root of $P_{q_i}$ is a simple root of this tail system; its first simple root is $\delta_i$. Finally $R(\delta_{i-1})\cdots R(\delta_1)\sigma=q_i$ by cancellation, so $\delta_i$ is the first root of $P_\sigma$ in the moved space in (4)(i), and $\delta_1=\tau_1$. This proves (4)(i). [F5, step 4.2, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.11.1: 11.1 The tuple $\theta_1<\cdots<\theta_k$ has reverse product $\sigma\le_Tc$ of length $k$, so it is among the tuples in (4)(iv). Let $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_k$ be any other such tuple. By step 2.3 every prefix $\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_r$ also has reverse product below $c$ of length $r$, so its $r$ roots are linearly independent. For each $s\ge r$, every root $\tau\in P_\sigma$ with $\tau<\theta_r$ has $\mu(\theta_s)\cdot\tau=0$: its pairing is nonnegative because $\tau$ is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and the restricted pairing functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)|_E$ are dual to $\Delta$ by step 8.2, while it is nonpositive by (2)(d). The restrictions to $E$ of the $k-r+1$ functionals $\mu(\theta_r),\dots,\mu(\theta_k)$ are independent, again by the dual-basis property. Their common kernel in $E$ therefore has dimension $r-1$. If $\eta_r<\theta_r$, the $r$ independent roots $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_r$ all lie in that kernel, a contradiction. Hence $\eta_r\ge\theta_r$ for every $r$, which proves componentwise domination (4)(vi) and the lexicographic minimality in (4)(iv). No Choice is used. [F4, F5, step 8.2, step 2.3, step 2.1, step 10.1] ∎

facts.fact_text: [F6] On the positive-definite space $(V,B)$, $M(A)=F(A)^\perp$ for orthogonal $A$. For $U\subseteq M(A)$ there is a unique orthogonal restriction $A_U\le_{\mathrm O}A$ with moved space $U$, and every line $L$ is the moved space of the unique orthogonal reflection $\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. For group elements, orthogonal order and reflection order agree by Carter's formula. [[lem-cg-orthogonal-wall-form-and-subspace-restriction]] (1),(3)-(5) [[thm-cg-carter-reflection-length-and-absolute-order]] (1),(2)

proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]

## Statement

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite, with $V=\mathbb R^S$, positive definite Coxeter form $B$, canonical reflection representation $\rho$, root system $\Phi$, reflection set $T$ and length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]), and let $\ell_T$, $M$, $F$ and $\le_T$ be as in [[def-cg-reflection-length-absolute-order-and-moved-space]]. Then:

**(1) Carter's formula.** For every $w\in W$,

$$\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)=\dim V-\dim F(w).$$

**(2) The absolute order.** $\le_T$ is a partial order on $W$ ([[def-partial-order]]), and:

**(i)** $u\le_T v$ holds if and only if there are reflections $t_1,\dots,t_m\in T$ and an index $k\le m$ such that $u=t_1\cdots t_k$ and $v=t_1\cdots t_m$ are shortest reflection factorizations, that is, $k=\ell_T(u)$ and $m=\ell_T(v)$ (a shortest reflection factorization of $u$ is a prefix of one of $v$);

**(ii)** $\ell_T(1)=0$, $u<_T v$ implies $\ell_T(u)<\ell_T(v)$, and $\ell_T(y)=\ell_T(x)+1$ whenever $y$ covers $x$; hence $\ell_T$ is a rank function and every interval $[u,v]_T=\{x\in W:u\le_Tx\le_Tv\}$ is finite ([[def-graded-poset-and-rank]]);

**(iii)** $|\ell_T(u)-\ell_T(v)|\le\ell_T(u^{-1}v)$, $\ell_T(u^{-1})=\ell_T(u)$ and $\ell_T(vuv^{-1})=\ell_T(u)$ for all $u,v\in W$;

**(iv)** $u\le_T v$ implies $M(u)\subseteq M(v)$ and $F(v)\subseteq F(u)$.

**(3) Moved-space rigidity under a common upper bound.** Let $\alpha,\beta,\delta\in W$ with $\alpha\le_T\delta$ and $\beta\le_T\delta$. Then

$$\alpha\le_T\beta\iff M(\alpha)\subseteq M(\beta);$$

in particular $M(\alpha)=M(\beta)$ implies $\alpha=\beta$, and $u\mapsto M(u)$ is an order isomorphism from $[1,\delta]_T$ onto its image ordered by inclusion. The proof of the converse uses the common upper bound $\delta$, through the restriction of $\delta$ to the subspace $M(\alpha)$; the converse is claimed only under this hypothesis (see the companion example of the $I_2(4)$ rotation, where the hypothesis fails).

facts.fact_text: [F10] For every nonzero point $x\in g\mathcal C_I$, its stabilizer is $gW_Ig^{-1}$. In a finite Coxeter system the chambers are translates of the simplicial fundamental chamber, whose inward unit normals are its simple roots. [[thm-cg-finite-chamber-tiling-and-coset-face-identification]] (1)-(3)

proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]

## Statement

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite, $n:=|S|$, and let the
arrangement $\mathcal A$, the chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$, the closed and open faces
$\overline{C_I}$ and $C_I$, the translated objects $wC$, $w\overline{C_I}$, $wC_I$, the unit
sphere $S^{n-1}$ and the coset face poset be as in
[[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]]. Let $\rho$,
$\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$, $V_+$, $T$, $\ell$ be as in
[[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]],
[[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]] and
[[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $S(u)$ denote the **support** of $u\in W$,
the set of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $u$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]], clause (1)); and let
$U=\bigcup_{w\in W}wC\subseteq V^*$ be the Tits cone of the dual action with its negative-root
sets $\operatorname{Neg}(f)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:f(\alpha)<0\}$
([[def-cg-tits-cone-and-fundamental-chamber]]). Then:

**(1) The chamber tiling.** $U=V^*$, and under the identification of the definition
$V=\bigcup_{w\in W}wC$; moreover
$$V\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}H_\alpha=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}wC^\circ,$$
the connected components of $V\setminus\bigcup_\alpha H_\alpha$ are exactly the sets
$wC^\circ$ $(w\in W)$ with closures $\overline{wC^\circ}=wC$, so the closed chambers of
$\mathcal A$ are exactly the sets $wC$; the map $w\mapsto wC^\circ$ is a bijection from $W$
onto the set of chambers, distinct closed chambers have disjoint interiors, and every
$W$-orbit in $V$ meets $C$ in exactly one point.

**(2) Simplicial chambers and their vertices.** Let $v_s\in V$ be the $B$-dual basis of
$(e_s)$, i.e. $B(v_s,e_t)=\delta_{st}$ ([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]],
[[thm-dual-family-is-a-basis-in-finite-dimension]]). Then
$$\overline{C_I}=\Bigl\{\sum_{s\notin I}\lambda_sv_s:\lambda_s\ge0\Bigr\},\qquad C_I=\Bigl\{\sum_{s\notin I}\lambda_sv_s:\lambda_s>0\Bigr\}$$
for every $I\subseteq S$; the closed chamber $C$ is the simplicial cone with extreme rays
$\mathbb R_{\ge0}v_s$ $(s\in S)$; the vertices of the spherical simplex $C\cap S^{n-1}$ are
exactly the points $v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B$, in the precise sense that
$C\cap S^{n-1}\cap\bigcap_{t\ne s}H_{e_t}=\{v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B\}$ for every $s$; and the dihedral angle
between the walls $H_{e_s}$ and $H_{e_t}$ is $\pi/m(s,t)$ in the following exact sense: the tangent
sector $\{v:B(v,e_s)\ge0,\ B(v,e_t)\ge0\}$ of $C$ along the codimension-two face
$C\cap H_{e_s}\cap H_{e_t}$ projects under the orthogonal projection
$V\to\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$ onto a sector in the two-plane $\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$
bounded by its two lines $H_{e_s}$ and $H_{e_t}$, and that sector has angle $\pi/m(s,t)$. More generally each $w\overline{C_I}$ is a simplicial cone with the linearly
independent generators $\rho(w)v_s$ $(s\notin I)$. The walls of the chamber $wC$ are the root
hyperplanes $wH_{e_s}=H_{\rho(w)e_s}$.

**(3) The face identification and the stabilisers.** The assignment
$wW_I\mapsto w\overline{C_I}$ is a well-defined bijection from the coset face poset onto the
set of proper faces $\{w\overline{C_I}:w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S\}$ (the remaining sets
$w\overline{C_S}$ are all equal to $\{0\}$, the common face of all chambers), and for all
$w,v\in W$ and $I,J\subseteq S$
$$wW_I=vW_J\iff w\overline{C_I}=v\overline{C_J},\qquad wW_I\subseteq vW_J\iff v\overline{C_J}\subseteq w\overline{C_I},$$
$$w\overline{C_I}\cap v\overline{C_J}=w\overline{C_{I\cup J\cup S(v^{-1}w)}},\qquad wC_I\cap vC_J\neq\emptyset\iff wW_I=vW_J,$$
so the relative interiors of the faces partition $V$; moreover
$V\setminus\{0\}=\bigsqcup wC_I$, the disjoint union running over the cosets $wW_I$ with
$I\subsetneq S$. For every $x\in wC_I$ one has
$\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=wW_Iw^{-1}$, and the setwise stabiliser
$\{w'\in W:w'w\overline{C_I}=w\overline{C_I}\}$ of the face $w\overline{C_I}$ is the same
subgroup $wW_Iw^{-1}$.

**(4) The spherical triangulation.** Assume $n\ge1$. Then
$S^{n-1}=\bigsqcup(wC_I\cap S^{n-1})$, the union running over the cosets $wW_I$ with
$I\subsetneq S$, and
$$\Sigma:=\{w\overline{C_I}\cap S^{n-1}:w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S\}$$
is the set of nonempty faces of a finite spherical simplicial complex (adjoin the empty face): each member is the spherical simplex whose
vertices are the points $\rho(w)v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B$ $(s\notin I)$ in the same sense, the relative interiors
$wC_I\cap S^{n-1}$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $S^{n-1}$, and the intersection of two
members is a common face, possibly empty, by (3); its face poset is isomorphic to the coset face poset by
$wW_I\mapsto w\overline{C_I}\cap S^{n-1}$. Consequently the abstract simplicial complex $K$
with vertices the cosets $wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ $(w\in W,\ s\in S)$ and simplices the empty set and the sets
$\{wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}:s\notin I\}$ $(w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S)$ is a triangulation of
$S^{n-1}$: the radial normalization $\varphi:|K|\to S^{n-1}$ of the simplexwise affine map into $V$ that sends the barycentric
coordinate at the vertex $wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ to the direction of $\rho(w)v_s$ is a
continuous bijection, $|K|$ is compact because $K$ is finite
([[prop-a-finite-simplicial-complex-has-compact-hausdorff-realization]]) and $S^{n-1}$ is
Hausdorff, so $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism
([[def-geometric-realization-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). In
particular $K$ has exactly $|W|$ maximal simplices, indexed by the chambers. For $S=\emptyset$
the group is trivial, $V=0$, and $S^{-1}=\emptyset$ is triangulated by the complex with no vertices and sole simplex $\emptyset$, whose realization is empty.

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type with $S$ finite, $n:=|S|$, and let the
arrangement $\mathcal A$, the chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$, the closed and open faces
$\overline{C_I}$ and $C_I$, the translated objects $wC$, $w\overline{C_I}$, $wC_I$, the unit
sphere $S^{n-1}$ and the coset face poset be as in
[[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]]. Let $\rho$,
$\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$, $V_+$, $T$, $\ell$ be as in
[[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]],
[[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]] and
[[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; let $S(u)$ denote the **support** of $u\in W$,
the set of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $u$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]], clause (1)); and let
$U=\bigcup_{w\in W}wC\subseteq V^*$ be the Tits cone of the dual action with its negative-root
sets $\operatorname{Neg}(f)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:f(\alpha)<0\}$
([[def-cg-tits-cone-and-fundamental-chamber]]). Then:

**(1) The chamber tiling.** $U=V^*$, and under the identification of the definition
$V=\bigcup_{w\in W}wC$; moreover
$$V\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}H_\alpha=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}wC^\circ,$$
the connected components of $V\setminus\bigcup_\alpha H_\alpha$ are exactly the sets
$wC^\circ$ $(w\in W)$ with closures $\overline{wC^\circ}=wC$, so the closed chambers of
$\mathcal A$ are exactly the sets $wC$; the map $w\mapsto wC^\circ$ is a bijection from $W$
onto the set of chambers, distinct closed chambers have disjoint interiors, and every
$W$-orbit in $V$ meets $C$ in exactly one point.

**(2) Simplicial chambers and their vertices.** Let $v_s\in V$ be the $B$-dual basis of
$(e_s)$, i.e. $B(v_s,e_t)=\delta_{st}$ ([[def-dual-family-associated-to-a-basis]],
[[thm-dual-family-is-a-basis-in-finite-dimension]]). Then
$$\overline{C_I}=\Bigl\{\sum_{s\notin I}\lambda_sv_s:\lambda_s\ge0\Bigr\},\qquad C_I=\Bigl\{\sum_{s\notin I}\lambda_sv_s:\lambda_s>0\Bigr\}$$
for every $I\subseteq S$; the closed chamber $C$ is the simplicial cone with extreme rays
$\mathbb R_{\ge0}v_s$ $(s\in S)$; the vertices of the spherical simplex $C\cap S^{n-1}$ are
exactly the points $v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B$, in the precise sense that
$C\cap S^{n-1}\cap\bigcap_{t\ne s}H_{e_t}=\{v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B\}$ for every $s$; and the dihedral angle
between the walls $H_{e_s}$ and $H_{e_t}$ is $\pi/m(s,t)$ in the following exact sense: the tangent
sector $\{v:B(v,e_s)\ge0,\ B(v,e_t)\ge0\}$ of $C$ along the codimension-two face
$C\cap H_{e_s}\cap H_{e_t}$ projects under the orthogonal projection
$V\to\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$ onto a sector in the two-plane $\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$
bounded by its two lines $H_{e_s}$ and $H_{e_t}$, and that sector has angle $\pi/m(s,t)$. More generally each $w\overline{C_I}$ is a simplicial cone with the linearly
independent generators $\rho(w)v_s$ $(s\notin I)$. The walls of the chamber $wC$ are the root
hyperplanes $wH_{e_s}=H_{\rho(w)e_s}$.

**(3) The face identification and the stabilisers.** The assignment
$wW_I\mapsto w\overline{C_I}$ is a well-defined bijection from the coset face poset onto the
set of proper faces $\{w\overline{C_I}:w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S\}$ (the remaining sets
$w\overline{C_S}$ are all equal to $\{0\}$, the common face of all chambers), and for all
$w,v\in W$ and $I,J\subseteq S$
$$wW_I=vW_J\iff w\overline{C_I}=v\overline{C_J},\qquad wW_I\subseteq vW_J\iff v\overline{C_J}\subseteq w\overline{C_I},$$
$$w\overline{C_I}\cap v\overline{C_J}=w\overline{C_{I\cup J\cup S(v^{-1}w)}},\qquad wC_I\cap vC_J\neq\emptyset\iff wW_I=vW_J,$$
so the relative interiors of the faces partition $V$; moreover
$V\setminus\{0\}=\bigsqcup wC_I$, the disjoint union running over the cosets $wW_I$ with
$I\subsetneq S$. For every $x\in wC_I$ one has
$\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=wW_Iw^{-1}$, and the setwise stabiliser
$\{w'\in W:w'w\overline{C_I}=w\overline{C_I}\}$ of the face $w\overline{C_I}$ is the same
subgroup $wW_Iw^{-1}$.

**(4) The spherical triangulation.** Assume $n\ge1$. Then
$S^{n-1}=\bigsqcup(wC_I\cap S^{n-1})$, the union running over the cosets $wW_I$ with
$I\subsetneq S$, and
$$\Sigma:=\{w\overline{C_I}\cap S^{n-1}:w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S\}$$
is the set of nonempty faces of a finite spherical simplicial complex (adjoin the empty face): each member is the spherical simplex whose
vertices are the points $\rho(w)v_s/\lVert v_s\rVert_B$ $(s\notin I)$ in the same sense, the relative interiors
$wC_I\cap S^{n-1}$ are pairwise disjoint and cover $S^{n-1}$, and the intersection of two
members is a common face, possibly empty, by (3); its face poset is isomorphic to the coset face poset by
$wW_I\mapsto w\overline{C_I}\cap S^{n-1}$. Consequently the abstract simplicial complex $K$
with vertices the cosets $wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ $(w\in W,\ s\in S)$ and simplices the empty set and the sets
$\{wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}:s\notin I\}$ $(w\in W,\ I\subsetneq S)$ is a triangulation of
$S^{n-1}$: the radial normalization $\varphi:|K|\to S^{n-1}$ of the simplexwise affine map into $V$ that sends the barycentric
coordinate at the vertex $wW_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ to the direction of $\rho(w)v_s$ is a
continuous bijection, $|K|$ is compact because $K$ is finite
([[prop-a-finite-simplicial-complex-has-compact-hausdorff-realization]]) and $S^{n-1}$ is
Hausdorff, so $\varphi$ is a homeomorphism
([[def-geometric-realization-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). In
particular $K$ has exactly $|W|$ maximal simplices, indexed by the chambers. For $S=\emptyset$
the group is trivial, $V=0$, and $S^{-1}=\emptyset$ is triangulated by the complex with no vertices and sole simplex $\emptyset$, whose realization is empty.

supplier_clause_note: Finite W: Statement1 U=V*/finite chamber tiling;2 dual-basis simplicial faces/angles;3 coset-face dictionary and point/setwise parabolic stabilizers, with origin separated;4 spherical triangulation, empty rank explicit.

note: Current exact-use review: F3→steps1.1,1.4,1.5,1.6,2.2,2.3,3.2,4.1,7.2,8.1,8.2,9.1,10.1, F13→steps7.2, F14→steps3.2,4.1. Irreducible finite rankn>=2, sigma<=c. Carter rigidity is used with common bound c. Transported normals span moved space for reduced reflection factorizations. Intrinsic parabolics/strong exchange identify subgroup roots, and rank-two formulas are instantiated to the restricted canonical system. Supplier interface: Statement1 positive roots↔T with conjugation and±normal uniqueness;2 |N(w)|=ell(w), prefix roots N(w^−1), suffix roots N(w);3 strong exchange for genuine t∈T with length descent.

facts.fact_text: [F3] $B$ is positive definite, every root has $B$-norm $1$, reflections act by $r_\alpha(x)=x-2B(x,\alpha)\alpha$, and $B(Cx,Cy)=B(x,y)$. For each positive root $\alpha$ there is a unique reflection $t_\alpha$ with $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$; its moved space is $\mathbb R\alpha$. [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]] (3) [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (2),(3) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1) [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]] (2)

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For every $i\ge1$, [F2] gives $(C-\mathrm{id})\mu_i=-2\rho_i$. Since $C$ is an isometry and $B(\rho_i,\rho_i)=1$, $B(\mu_i,\rho_i)=1$ follows by expanding $B(C\mu_i,C\mu_i)=B(\mu_i-2\rho_i,\mu_i-2\rho_i)$. The same identity gives $C\mu_i=\mu_i-2\rho_i$, so $r_{\rho_i}C\mu_i=\mu_i$ and $\mu_i\in F(r_{\rho_i}C)$. For $1\le i\le n$, the reflection word $r_{\rho_i}C$ cancels to $R_1\cdots R_{i-1}R_{i+1}\cdots R_n$, so its reflection length is at most $n-1$; the triangle inequality and $\ell_T(c)=n$ give the lower bound $n-1$. Thus its fixed space is one-dimensional. Since $r_{\rho_{i+n}}C=C(r_{\rho_i}C)C^{-1}$, the same dimension holds for all $i$. The vector $\mu_i$ is nonzero because $\mu_i\cdot\rho_i=1$, and it is the unique vector in that line with this pairing. This proves (1). [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.4: 1.4 Every reflection lies below $c$. Indeed, $M(c)=V$ by [F1]. For a positive root $\alpha$, the orthogonal reflection with moved line $\mathbb R\alpha$ is uniquely $r_\alpha=\rho(t_\alpha)$ by [F3],[F6]; the Wall restriction for this line is below $C=\rho(c)$ and has moved space $\mathbb R\alpha$. The Wall dimension identity and Carter's formula therefore give $t_\alpha\le_Tc$. [F1, F3, F5, F6]
proof_step_texts.1.5: 1.5 We use two elementary consequences of absolute order. First, if $w=r_1\cdots r_m$ is a reduced reflection factorization and $p<q$, then $r_pr_q\le_Tw$: distinct root-reflections have product moved space the two-plane spanned by their distinct normal lines, so their product has reflection length $2$ by Carter's formula. Write $w=xr_pyr_qz$; then $(r_pr_q)^{-1}w=r_qr_pxr_pyr_qz=(r_q(r_pxr_p)y r_q)z$, a product of $m-2$ reflections because conjugation preserves reflections. The triangle inequality forces this complement to have length $m-2$. Second, if $u\le_Tv\le_Tw$, then $v^{-1}w\le_Tu^{-1}w$: write $v=ux$, $w=vy$ with additive reflection lengths; then $u^{-1}w=xy$, while $y^{-1}xy$ has the same length as $x$, so $y\le_Txy$. These facts will be used below. [F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.1.6: 1.6 Put $E=M(\sigma)$ and $F=E^\perp$. Then $W_\sigma=\{w:M(w)\subseteq E\}$ is the pointwise stabilizer of $F$, because $M(w)=F(w)^\perp$. If $F\ne0$, choose $x\in F$ outside $\{0\}$ and every proper subspace $F\cap H_\alpha$; this is possible by [F9] and [F12]. By [F10], $\operatorname{Stab}_W(x)=gW_Ig^{-1}$ for some $g,I$. Each conjugate simple generator has a root hyperplane containing $x$, hence, by the choice of $x$, containing all of $F$; therefore every generator of this stabilizer fixes $F$ pointwise. Conversely every element fixing $F$ fixes $x$, so $W_\sigma=gW_Ig^{-1}$. If $F=0$, take $g=1$ and $I=S$. [F3, F5, F9, F10, F12]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 For every $\sigma\le_Tc$, one has $P_\sigma=\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$. If $\alpha\in P_\sigma$, then $M(t_\alpha)=\mathbb R\alpha\subseteq M(\sigma)$ by [F5]. Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+\cap M(\sigma)$, then $t_\alpha\le_Tc$ by step 1.4 and $\sigma\le_Tc$, so moved-space rigidity in [F5] gives $t_\alpha\le_T\sigma$. Also $P_\sigma$ spans $M(\sigma)$: choose a reduced reflection factorization of $\sigma$; its prefix-conjugated normals are a basis of $M(\sigma)$ by [F7], and the reflections with those normals have moved lines in $M(\sigma)$, hence lie below $\sigma$ by the same common-upper-bound argument. Taking the positive sign of each normal puts a spanning set in $P_\sigma$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, step 1.4]
proof_step_texts.2.3: 2.3 For any increasing tuple $a_1<\cdots<a_m$ of positive roots, one has $\ell_T(R(a_1)\cdots R(a_m)c)=n-m$ if and only if $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$ for all $i>j$. If $m=0$, the left side is $\ell_T(c)=n$ by [F1], and the zero-pairing condition is vacuous; hence assume $m\ge1$. Put $r_i=R(a_i)$. The length equality is equivalent to the reverse product $q=r_m\cdots r_1$ being a reduced element below $c$: its complement is $q^{-1}c=r_1\cdots r_m c$. In fact, if $\ell_T(q^{-1}c)=n-m$, then $\ell_T(q)\le m$ and $n=\ell_T(c)\le\ell_T(q)+\ell_T(q^{-1}c)\le n$, so both inequalities are equalities; the converse is the defining absolute-order equality. For the forward implication, the pair-product fact in step 1.5 gives $r_i r_j\le_Tc$ whenever $i>j$. Since $\ell_T(r_i c)=n-1$, this gives $r_j\le_Tr_i c$ from $\ell_T(r_j r_i c)=n-2$; hence $M(r_j)\subseteq M(r_i c)=F(r_i c)^\perp$. The vector $\mu(a_i)$ is a nonzero member of the one-dimensional fixed space $F(r_i c)$, so $\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j=0$. Conversely, suppose all these pairings vanish. The matrix $[\mu(a_i)\cdot a_j]$ is upper triangular with diagonal $1$ by (1), so both the $a_i$ and the $\mu(a_i)$ are linearly independent; in particular $m\le n$. Induct downward on $i$ to prove $q_i:=r_m\cdots r_i\le_Tc$ with length $m-i+1$. The base $q_m=r_m$ is step 1.4. If $q_{i+1}\le_Tc$, then each factor $r_j$ with $j>i$ satisfies $r_j\le_Tq_{i+1}$: writing a reduced factorization $q_{i+1}=x r_j y$, the product $r_jq_{i+1}=(r_jxr_j)y$ uses one fewer reflections, and the triangle inequality makes that expression reduced. Put $v=q_{i+1}^{-1}c$. Complement order reversal from step 1.5 gives $v\le_Tr_jc$, so $\mu(a_j)\in F(r_jc)\subseteq F(v)$ for every $j>i$. These $m-i$ independent vectors form a basis of $F(v)$, whose dimension is $m-i$ by Carter's formula. The assumed zero pairings give $a_i\in F(v)^\perp=M(v)$. The Wall restriction for the line $\mathbb Ra_i$ gives $r_i\le_Tv$; writing $v=r_i z$ then gives $c=q_{i+1}r_i z$, with lengths adding, so $q_i=q_{i+1}r_i\le_Tc$ and $\ell_T(q_i)=m-i+1$. At $i=1$ this proves the claimed equivalence. The same argument applies to every subtuple because the vanishing conditions are inherited. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.4, step 1.5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]
proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.1: 8.1 Suppose $\ell_T(\sigma)=2$ and $P_\sigma=\{\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_t\}$. By (4)(i), $\Delta=\{\tau_1,\tau_t\}$ and $\sigma=R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)$. Step 4.1 realizes this as a canonical rank-two system. If its exponent is $m$, [F11] gives simple-root angle $\pi-\pi/m$ and a rotation of magnitude $2\pi/m$. Write its generators as $r,s$ and $q=rs$. The identities $rqr=q^{-1}$ and $s=rq$ reduce every word to $q^j$ or $q^jr$, $0\le j<m$; their distinct actions are the $m$ rotations and $m$ reflections in lines spaced by $\pi/m$. Every reflection is a conjugate of $r$ or $s$: the conjugates give respectively $q^{2j}r$ and $q^{2j-1}r$. The root-reflection dictionary thus gives $t=m$ positive roots, equally spaced between the simple-root rays. The global order agrees with angular order: a decrease after $\tau_r$ would put $\tau_{r+1}$ in the cone on earlier roots $\tau_1,\tau_r$, contrary to step 3.1. A product of reflections has rotation angle twice the difference of its normal angles, modulo $2\pi$; hence the two-reflection factorizations of $\sigma$ are exactly $R(\tau_1)R(\tau_t)=R(\tau_2)R(\tau_1)=\cdots=R(\tau_t)R(\tau_{t-1})$. These exhaust factorizations in $W$: if $\sigma=R(\alpha)R(\beta)$, then $M(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(\alpha,\beta)$, and both spaces have dimension $2$, so the positive representatives of $\alpha,\beta$ lie in $P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. The endpoint angle gives $\tau_1\cdot\tau_t=-\cos(\pi/t)\le0$, while each adjacent angle gives $\tau_i\cdot\tau_{i+1}=\cos(\pi/t)\ge0$. [F3, F5, F11, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, algebra]
proof_step_texts.8.2: 8.2 Fix $i$. The second factorization in (4)(ii) writes $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_i)q_i'$ where $q_i'$ is the product of the other $k-1$ simple reflections in $\Delta$. Thus $\ell_T(q_i')=k-1$, $R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma$, and $q_i'=R(\varepsilon_i)\sigma$. Since $c=\sigma v$ with $\ell_T(v)=n-k$, $R(\varepsilon_i)c=q_i'v$ is reduced, so $q_i'\le_TR(\varepsilon_i)c$. It follows that $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\in F(q_i')$. The moved space $M(q_i')$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}\{\delta_j:j\ne i\}$: it is contained there because those are its reflection normals, and both dimensions are $k-1$. Hence $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_j=0$ for $j\ne i$. Since $\varepsilon_i-\delta_i$ is a linear combination of $\delta_1,\dots,\delta_{i-1}$, (1) gives $1=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\varepsilon_i=\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot\delta_i$. Thus the restrictions to $E$ of the functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)$ form the dual basis to $\Delta$. For $x=\sum_j a_j\delta_j$ with $a_j\ge0$, $\mu(\varepsilon_i)\cdot x=a_i$; intersecting the cone with this zero hyperplane and with the unit sphere proves the wall equality, and the supporting hyperplane in $E$ is $E\cap\mu(\varepsilon_i)^\perp$. This proves (4)(iii). [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 7.2, algebra]
proof_step_texts.9.1: 9.1 If distinct positive roots $\rho_i,\rho_j$ satisfy $R(\rho_i)R(\rho_j)\le_Tc$, their product has reflection length $2$ and belongs to the rank-two case of step 8.1. Both roots lie in the corresponding $P_\sigma$ by moved-space rigidity. If $i<j$, the only increasing-order two-factorization in step 8.1 is the endpoint factorization, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\le0$. If $i>j$, the factorization is one of the adjacent descending pairs, so $\rho_i\cdot\rho_j\ge0$. This proves (4)(v). [F3, F5, step 8.1]
proof_step_texts.10.1: 10.1 If $i<j$ and $\varepsilon_i>\varepsilon_j$, the factorization $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$ is reduced, and the pair-product fact of step 1.5 gives $R(\varepsilon_j)R(\varepsilon_i)\le_T\sigma\le_Tc$. The rank-two sign result of step 9.1 gives $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j\le0$. On the other hand, since distinct simple roots have nonpositive pairings by step 4.1, applying $R(\delta_{j-1}),\dots,R(\delta_{i+1})$ successively to $\delta_j$ yields a nonnegative combination of $\delta_{i+1},\dots,\delta_j$, and $\varepsilon_i\cdot\varepsilon_j=-\delta_i\cdot(R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_{j-1})\delta_j)\ge0$. Thus the pairing is zero, and the two reflections commute. Sorting the $\varepsilon_i$ into global order uses only swaps of such inverted commuting pairs, so the product is unchanged and $\sigma=R(\theta_k)\cdots R(\theta_1)$. [F3, step 4.1, step 7.2, step 1.5, step 9.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F13] For a reduced simple-generator expression $w=s_1\cdots s_m$, every prefix-conjugated normal $\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})e_{s_i}$ is a positive root. [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (2)

proof_step_texts.7.2: 7.2 Put $D_i:=R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_{i-1})$ and $\varepsilon_i:=D_i\delta_i$. The prefix $R(\delta_1)\cdots R(\delta_i)$ has reflection length $i$ by the factorization of $\sigma$ and the triangle inequality, so this simple-generator word in the Coxeter system of $W_\sigma$ is reduced. The root-inversion formula [F13], applied to that parabolic system, gives $\varepsilon_i\in P_\sigma$, hence it is a positive root. Conjugation gives $R(\varepsilon_i)=D_iR(\delta_i)D_i^{-1}$; multiplying these identities and cancelling adjacent inverse prefixes yields $\sigma=R(\varepsilon_k)\cdots R(\varepsilon_1)$. Also $R(\varepsilon_i)D_iR(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=D_iR(\delta_i)R(\delta_{i+1})\cdots R(\delta_k)=\sigma$. This proves (4)(ii). [F3, F5, F13, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

facts.fact_text: [F14] $(W_I,I)$ is the Coxeter system of the restricted matrix, with intrinsic length equal to ambient length; every element of $W_I$ has a reduced expression using only letters of $I$. If $t\in T$ and $\ell(tw)<\ell(w)$, strong exchange expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of one letter of any reduced expression of $w$. [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1)-(2) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (3)

proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]

## Statement

Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group with length $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$ with Coxeter form $B$, canonical reflection homomorphism $\rho$, root system $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$ and reflection set $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]]); every root has $B$-norm one.

**(1) The root-reflection dictionary.** For $\alpha\in\Phi$ choose $w\in W$, $s\in S$ with $\alpha=\rho(w)e_s$ and put $t_\alpha:=wsw^{-1}\in T$. Then:
(i) $t_\alpha$ is independent of the chosen representation of $\alpha$;
(ii) $\rho(t_\alpha)=r_\alpha$, the reflection with normal $\alpha$; and $t_{\rho(w)\alpha}=w\,t_\alpha\,w^{-1}$ for all $w\in W$, $\alpha\in\Phi$;
(iii) $t_{-\alpha}=t_\alpha$, and for $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ one has $t_\alpha=t_\beta$ if and only if $\alpha=\pm\beta$;
(iv) the induced map $\{\pm\alpha:\alpha\in\Phi\}\to T$ is a bijection; so is the map $\Phi_+\to T$, $\alpha\mapsto t_\alpha$.

**(2) Inversion formula.** For every $w\in W$ one has $|N(w)|=\ell(w)$ (with $N$ as in [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]]); and for every reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_n$,
$$N(w)=\bigl\{\rho(s_{i+1}\cdots s_n)^{-1}e_{s_i}:1\le i\le n\bigr\},\qquad N(w^{-1})=\bigl\{\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})e_{s_i}:1\le i\le n\bigr\},$$
the displayed elements being pairwise distinct positive roots.

**(3) Strong exchange.** Let $w\in W$ and $t\in T$ satisfy $\ell(tw)<\ell(w)$, and let $w=s_1\cdots s_n$ be a reduced expression. Then there is a unique $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ with
$$tw=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_n,\qquad t=r_i:=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1;$$
moreover, if $\alpha\in\Phi_+$ is the positive root with $t=t_\alpha$, then $\alpha\in N(w^{-1})$ and $\alpha=\rho(s_1\cdots s_{i-1})e_{s_i}$.

For each $s\ge r$, every root $\tau\in P_\sigma$ with $\tau<\theta_r$ has $\mu(\theta_s)\cdot\tau=0$: its pairing is nonnegative because $\tau$ is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$ and the restricted pairing functionals $B(\mu(\varepsilon_i),-)|_E$ are dual to $\Delta$ by step 8.2, while it is nonpositive by (2)(d). Hence $\eta_r\ge\theta_r$ for every $r$, which proves componentwise domination (4)(vi) and the lexicographic minimality in (4)(iv). No Choice is used. ## Statement

Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$ with Coxeter form $B$, the reflections $r_a$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), the canonical reflection homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the root system $\Phi=\{\rho(w)e_s\}$, the reflections $T$, and the positive cone $V_+=\{\sum_s\lambda_se_s:\lambda_s\ge0\}$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]); every root satisfies $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$ ([[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]] (3)). Let $C,C^\circ$ be the chamber and its interior of the dual action and put $B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\}$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]).

**(1) Sign criterion for the cone.** For $v\in V$: $v\in V_+\setminus\{0\}$ if and only if $f(v)>0$ for every $f\in C^\circ$.

**(2) Roots have a sign.** Every root $\alpha\in\Phi$ lies in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$ or in $-V_+\setminus\{0\}$, and not in both. Hence, with
$$\Phi_+:=\Phi\cap V_+,\qquad \Phi_-:=\Phi\cap(-V_+),$$
one has $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$, $\Phi_-=-\Phi_+$, $e_s\in\Phi_+$ for every $s\in S$, and for every $w\in W$ and $s\in S$
$$\rho(w)e_s\in\Phi_+\iff w^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq B_s,\qquad \rho(w)e_s\in\Phi_-\iff w^{-1}C^\circ\subseteq sB_s.$$
In particular $f(\alpha)>0$ for all $f\in C^\circ$ when $\alpha\in\Phi_+$, and $f(\alpha)<0$ for all $f\in C^\circ$ when $\alpha\in\Phi_-$.

**(3) Simple reflections act on positive roots.** For every $s\in S$,
$$r_s(\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\})=\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\},\qquad r_se_s=-e_s,\qquad r_s\Phi=\Phi;$$
equivalently $r_s\Phi_+=(\Phi_+\setminus\{e_s\})\cup\{-e_s\}$.

[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1)-(2) [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (3)

proof_step_texts.3.2: 3.2 Let $\Phi_I=\{\rho(u)\alpha_s:u\in W_I,s\in I\}$ be the intrinsic root system from [F14]; its representation is the restriction to $V_I=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_s:s\in I\}$, since the reflection formulas agree. An ambient reflection $t\in T\cap W_I$ has a reduced $I$-expression by [F14]. Apply strong exchange to $tt=1$: it expresses $t$ as a prefix-conjugate of a letter of that expression, so its root normal belongs to $\pm\Phi_I$ by [F3]. Conversely every intrinsic root gives an ambient reflection in $W_I$. Conjugating by $g$, the root-reflection dictionary therefore identifies the roots of $gW_Ig^{-1}$ with precisely the ambient roots whose reflections fix $F$ pointwise, namely $\Phi\cap E=\pm P_\sigma$ by step 2.2. Their span is both $\rho(g)V_I$ and $E$, since $P_\sigma$ spans $E$. [F3, F14, step 2.2, step 1.6]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 Choose $f\in\mathcal C^\circ$ and project it orthogonally to $E$. Its pairing with every root of $P_\sigma$ is positive by [F4], so it avoids the subsystem arrangement. Apply [F10] to the finite Coxeter system $(W_I,I)$ and transfer its chambers to $E$ by $\rho(g)$. The chamber containing the projection has inward unit normals $\Delta=\{\rho(gu)\alpha_s:s\in I\}$ for some $u\in W_I$. These are a basis of $E$, their reflections are the conjugates of the simple generators of $W_I$, and their Gram matrix is the restricted Coxeter Gram matrix. In particular distinct normals have nonpositive pairings. By the root-sign theorem [F4] applied to this conjugate Coxeter system, its positive roots are exactly the roots positive on the projection, hence $P_\sigma$, and every such root is a nonnegative combination of $\Delta$. This supplies the simple system and the Coxeter presentation used below. [F3, F4, F10, F14, step 3.2]

supplier_current_claim:
## Statement

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

supplier_current_claim:
## Definition

Let $S$ be a finite set and let $m$ be a Coxeter matrix on $S$, so that $m(s,s)=1$ and $m(s,t)=m(t,s)\in\{2,3,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ for $s\ne t$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]).

**(1) The space and its distinguished functions.** Let $V:=\mathbb R^S$ be the real vector space of all functions $S\to\mathbb R$, with pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]]); it is a vector space over the ordered field $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]]). Write $u(s)$ for the value of $u$ at $s$ and put $e_s(s):=1$, $e_s(t):=0$ for $t\ne s$.

**(2) The Coxeter form.** For finite $m(s,t)$ put $c(s,t):=\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ ([[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]]) and for $m(s,t)=\infty$ put $c(s,t):=1$; then $c(s,t)=c(t,s)$ and $c(s,s)=\cos\pi=-1$. The **Coxeter form** $B$ is the unique symmetric bilinear form on $V$ with $B(e_s,e_t)=-c(s,t)$ for all $s,t\in S$; in particular $B(e_s,e_s)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-\cos(\pi/m(s,t))$ for finite $m(s,t)$, while $B(e_s,e_t)=-1$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], [[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]]). **No positive definiteness, definiteness or nondegeneracy of $B$ is presumed**: $\operatorname{rad}(B):=\{u:B(u,v)=0\text{ for all }v\in V\}$ may be nonzero ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and the form may be indefinite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]). A linear map $g:V\to V$ is **$B$-preserving** when $B(gu,gw)=B(u,w)$ for all $u,w\in V$.

**(3) Reflections.** For $a\in V$ with $B(a,a)\ne0$ define the **reflection with normal $a$** by $$r_a(v):=v-\frac{2B(v,a)}{B(a,a)}a .$$ The definition asserts neither that $r_a$ is linear or an involution nor that $\ker B(-,a)=\{v:B(v,a)=0\}$ is a hyperplane; these are proved in [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]]. When $B(a,a)=0$ the symbol $r_a$ is not defined.
supplier_clause_note: Definition1 finite coordinate basis;2 diagonal1/off-diagonal −cos with infinity coefficient1, no ambient nondegeneracy assumed;3 reflection divides by B(a,a) and is undefined for null normals.

facts.fact_text: [F5] $B$ is symmetric and bilinear, and positive definite: $B(u,u)\ge0$ with $B(u,u)=0$ only for $u=0$; consequently $B$ is nondegenerate, so $B(x,y)=0$ for all $y\in V$ implies $x=0$, and the same holds for the restriction of $B$ to any subspace. [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] [[thm-cg-finite-type-positive-definite-criterion]]

proof_step_texts.1.1: 1.1 For $y\in V$ one has $B((A-\mathrm{id})x,y)=B(x,(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y)$ for all $x\in V$ by [F4], so $y\in M(A)^\perp$ holds exactly when $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})y=0$ and hence exactly when $A^{-1}y=y$, that is, when $y\in F(A^{-1})$; thus $M(A)^\perp=F(A^{-1})$. Since $A^{-1}y=y$ holds exactly when $Ay=y$, one has $F(A^{-1})=F(A)$, and $A^{-1}-\mathrm{id}=-A^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})$ shows $M(A^{-1})=M(A)$. Consequently $M(A)^\perp=F(A)$, and [F2] gives $M(A)=M(A)^{\perp\perp}=F(A)^\perp$, $V=M(A)\oplus F(A)$ and $\dim M(A)+\dim F(A)=\dim V$. Moreover $A(A-\mathrm{id})=(A-\mathrm{id})A$, so $A(M(A))=M(A)$; and $A(F(A))\subseteq F(A)$ with equality because $A$ is injective. [F2, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.2.2: 2.2 Let $A\in\mathrm O(V)$ with $\dim M(A)=1$, put $L:=M(A)$ and let $\Pi_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $L$ [F3]. By step 1.1 the line $L$ and the space $F(A)=L^\perp$ are $A$-stable, so $A$ fixes $L^\perp$ pointwise; for $0\ne u\in L$ one has $Au=cu$ with $c\in\mathbb R$, and since $A$ preserves $B$ by [F4] and $B(u,u)\ne0$ by [F5], $c^2B(u,u)=B(Au,Au)=B(u,u)$ forces $c^2=1$, while $c=1$ would put $u\in L\cap F(A)=\{0\}$; hence $c=-1$ and $A=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. Conversely if $L$ is a line then $A':=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$ acts as $-1$ on $L$ and as the identity on $L^\perp$, so it preserves $B$ and is invertible, and $M(A')=L$ has dimension one; if $A'\in\mathrm O(V)$ is a reflection with $M(A')=L$, the first part applied to $A'$ gives $A'=\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. Hence every line $L\subseteq V$ is the moved space of exactly one reflection of $\mathrm O(V)$, namely $\mathrm{id}-2\Pi_L$. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 Applying step 2.1 to the orthogonal element $A^{-1}$, whose moved space is $M(A)$ by step 1.1, gives the bijection $T_A:=((A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)})^{-1}:M(A)\to M(A)$. For $u,v\in M(A)$ put $w:=S_Au$ and $z:=T_Av$, so that $(A-\mathrm{id})w=u$ and $(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})z=v$; then $B(S_Au,v)=B(w,(A^{-1}-\mathrm{id})z)=B(w,A^{-1}z)-B(w,z)=B(Aw,z)-B(w,z)=B((A-\mathrm{id})w,z)=B(u,T_Av)$, using [F4] and symmetry of $B$. Moreover $A^{-1}-\mathrm{id}=-A^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})$ on the $A$-stable space $M(A)$, so the inverse there is $T_A=-S_AA$ and $S_A+T_A=S_A(\mathrm{id}-A)=-((A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)})^{-1}(A-\mathrm{id})|_{M(A)}=-\mathrm{id}_{M(A)}$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.4.1: 4.1 The Wall form $\chi_A(u,v)=B(S_Au,v)$ is bilinear on $M(A)$, and for $u,v\in M(A)$ the transpose identity of step 3.1 gives $B(S_Av,u)=B(v,T_Au)=B(T_Au,v)$, so $\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u)=B(S_Au,v)+B(T_Au,v)=B((S_A+T_A)u,v)=-B(u,v)$. If $\chi_A(u,v)=0$ for all $v\in M(A)$, then $B(S_Au,\cdot)$ vanishes on $M(A)$ and, since $S_Au\in M(A)=F(A)^\perp$, also on $F(A)$, hence on $V$; by [F5] $S_Au=0$, and $S_A$ is injective, so $u=0$: the form $\chi_A$ is nondegenerate, and its symmetric part is $\tfrac12(\chi_A(u,v)+\chi_A(v,u))=-\tfrac12B(u,v)$ on $M(A)$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F4, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.5.1: 5.1 Let $U\subseteq M(A)$ and define $H_U:=\Pi_US_A|_U:U\to U$. For $u,v\in U$, [F3] gives $B(H_Uu,v)=B(S_Au,v)=\chi_A(u,v)$; if another operator has these pairings, its difference from $H_U$ pairs to zero with every $v\in U$, so it equals $H_U$ by [F5]. Define $H_U^t:=\Pi_UT_A|_U$, with $T_A$ from step 3.1. That step and [F3] give $B(H_U^tu,v)=B(T_Au,v)=B(u,S_Av)=B(u,H_Uv)$, so $H_U^t$ is the adjoint $H_U^*$ of [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]. Since $S_A+T_A=-\mathrm{id}_{M(A)}$, compression to $U$ gives $H_U+H_U^t=-\mathrm{id}_U$. If $H_Uu=0$, then $0=B(H_Uu,u)=\chi_A(u,u)=-\tfrac12B(u,u)$ by step 4.1, hence $u=0$; thus $H_U$ is injective and invertible by [F1], including when $U=0$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]
proof_step_texts.6.1: 6.1 Define $A_U\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ by $A_Uu=u+H_U^{-1}u$ for $u\in U$ and $A_U=\mathrm{id}$ on $U^\perp$; this is well defined and linear because $V=U\oplus U^\perp$ [F2]. Then $A_U-\mathrm{id}=H_U^{-1}\Pi_U$ has image $U$, so $M(A_U)=U$ and $(A_U-\mathrm{id})|_U^{-1}=H_U$. Put $T:=H_U^{-1}\in\mathrm{GL}(U)$ and $T^t:=(H_U^t)^{-1}$; inverting the transpose relation of step 5.1 shows that $T^t$ is the transpose of $T$, that is, $B(Tx,y)=B(x,T^ty)$ for all $x,y\in U$. Multiplying $H_U+H_U^t=-\mathrm{id}_U$ on the left by $T$ and on the right by $T^t$, and also on the left by $T^t$ and on the right by $T$, gives $T+T^t=-TT^t=-T^tT$, hence $(\mathrm{id}+T)(\mathrm{id}+T^t)=\mathrm{id}_U=(\mathrm{id}+T^t)(\mathrm{id}+T)$. Therefore $B(A_Uu,A_Uv)=B((\mathrm{id}+T^t)(\mathrm{id}+T)u,v)=B(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in U$, the transpose of $\mathrm{id}+T$ being $\mathrm{id}+T^t$; on $U^\perp$ the operator $A_U$ is the identity, and $U\perp U^\perp$, so $A_U$ preserves $B$ on $V$. If $A_Ux=0$, then $B(x,y)=B(A_Ux,A_Uy)=0$ for every $y\in V$, so $x=0$ by [F5] and $A_U$ is injective, hence invertible by [F1]: thus $A_U\in\mathrm O(V)$. [step 5.1, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

## Statement

Let $S$ be a finite set with Coxeter matrix $m$, presented group $W$, length
function $\ell$ and diagram $\Gamma$
([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]],
[[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]]); let $V=\mathbb R^S$
carry the Coxeter form $B$ with reflections $r_a$
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), let
$\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ be the canonical reflection homomorphism
([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic
dual with its dual action, the closed chamber $C$ and its interior $C^\circ$
([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]],
[[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]]).

**(1) Finiteness criterion.** $W$ is finite if and only if $B$ is positive
definite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

**(2) The dual form.** Assume $B$ is positive definite. Then
$b:V\to V^*$, $b(v):=B(v,\cdot)$, is a linear isomorphism, and
$B^*(f,g):=B(b^{-1}f,b^{-1}g)$ defines a positive definite symmetric bilinear
form $B^*$ on $V^*$; for every $w\in W$ the dual map $\rho^*(w)$ preserves
$B^*$: $B^*(w\cdot f,w\cdot g)=B^*(f,g)$ for all $f,g\in V^*$.

**(3) Isolation of the identity and discreteness.** For every $f\in C^\circ$
the set $\Omega_f:=\{h\in\mathrm{GL}(V^*):h\cdot f\in C^\circ\}$ is an open
neighbourhood of $\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$ in $\mathrm{GL}(V^*)$ and
$\Omega_f\cap\rho^*(W)=\{\mathrm{id}\}$. Consequently $\rho^*(W)$ is a discrete
subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(V^*)$, and $\rho(W)$ is a discrete subgroup of
$\mathrm{GL}(V)$. This clause uses no positive definiteness of $B$.

facts.fact_text: [F7] $\rho$ is a group homomorphism, so $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\rho(1)=\mathrm{id}_V$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]). $\ell_T(w)$ is the least $k$ over products of $k$ elements of $T$; $M(u)=M(\rho(u))$, $F(u)=F(\rho(u))$; and $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ with $(W,S)$ presented as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. Thus $M(t_1\cdots t_m)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\rho(t_1\cdots t_{i-1})M(t_i)$. [F7, algebra, given]
proof_step_texts.3.1: 3.1 Carter's formula and factorization: every $w\in W$ satisfies $\ell_T(w)=\dim M(w)$, and $w$ is a product of exactly $\dim M(w)$ elements of $T$. If $w=1$, then $\dim M(w)=0$ and the empty product represents $1$, giving both assertions. If $w\ne1$ with $\dim M(w)=k\ge1$, step 2.2 supplies $t:=t_\alpha\in T$ with $\dim M(tw)=k-1$; by induction on $k$ (applied to $tw$, whose moved dimension is $k-1$) there are $t_2,\dots,t_k\in T$ with $tw=t_2\cdots t_k$, so $w=t\cdot(tw)=tt_2\cdots t_k$ is a product of $k$ elements of $T$. For the reverse inequality let $w=s_1\cdots s_j$ with $s_1,\dots,s_j\in T$; then $k=\dim M(w)=\dim M(\rho(s_1)\cdots\rho(s_j))\le j$ by step 2.1, so no shorter product of elements of $T$ represents $w$ and $\ell_T(w)=k$ by [F7]. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F7]
